about.title: Our species, our cousins: Homo sapiens, Neanderthals and Denisovans
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. This class has six topics, two real disagreements, and four sites that each need two dates. The DNA beats and the two debates are the slowest parts. If you need a break, pause after the 'Two models of origin' beats, then after the Neanderthal DNA beats.

say.text: Welcome. Today we meet two groups of human cousins, the Neanderthals and the Denisovans. Then we ask where our own species came from.

show.text: Our species, our cousins

say.text: Here is a surprise to start. Seventy thousand years ago we were not alone. At least four kinds of human were alive.

show.text: Four human species: Homo luzonensis, Homo floresiensis, Homo neanderthalensis, Homo sapiens

ask.q: About 70,000 years ago, how many human species were alive?
ask.why: The Smithsonian says that just 70,000 years ago there were at least four human species on Earth.

say.text: Let's meet the closest cousin first. Neanderthals are our closest extinct human relative. The first fossils called Neanderthal were found in 1856, in Germany's Neander Valley.

show.text: Neanderthals

say.text: Their bodies were built for the cold. Short and stocky, with shorter lower arms and legs. That shape helps hold heat in.

show.text: A reconstructed Neanderthal skeleton: a broad chest and short lower arm and leg bones, shown next to a taller, leaner skeleton of an earlier human.

ask.q: Why would a short, broad body help in an Ice Age winter?
ask.right: It helps the body keep its heat in
ask.why: The Smithsonian explains that a short, broad body shape retains heat, which is useful in cold places.

say.text: Now their tools. The style is called Mousterian. The maker first prepared a stone core, then struck off flakes of a planned shape.

show.text: Mousterian: flakes struck from a prepared core

say.text: Those flakes did real work. Scrapers cleaned animal hides. Awls punched holes so strips could lace hides into loose clothing.

show.text: Scraper: cleans a hide; Awl: pokes holes in a hide; Thrusting spear: used for hunting large animals

ask.q: What was a scraper used for?
ask.why: The Smithsonian says a Neanderthal would probably use a scraper first to clean a hide, then an awl to make holes.

say.text: Where did they live? Across Europe and from south-west to central Asia, from about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. In warm spells they reached northern Germany.

show.text: A map of Europe and western to central Asia shaded as Neanderthal range, with the Neander Valley (Germany) and Shanidar Cave (Iraq) marked.

say.text: One famous Neanderthal place is Shanidar Cave, in Iraq. Caves are not built, so we give two dates: when people lived there, and when scientists found them.

show.text: 45,000 to 35,000 years ago: Shanidar 3 lived; 1953 to 1960: ten Neanderthals dug out of the cave; 1957: Shanidar 3 found

say.text: The cave held tools, hearths and signs of purposeful burial. But be careful. The museum says Shanidar 3 may have been buried by his group, or covered by a rock fall.

show.text: Buried by his group | Covered by a rock fall from the cave roof. The evidence cannot settle it.

ask.q: What is a fair summary of how Shanidar 3 came to be buried?
ask.right: Either his group buried him or a rock fall covered him; it is not certain
wrong: Proven: a ceremony by Homo sapiens
Proven: he was placed in a grave with gifts
ask.why: The Smithsonian says he may have been buried by members of his group or by a rock fall from the cave roof.

say.text: Now a cousin we first met through DNA. In 2008, diggers in Denisova Cave, in southern Siberia, found a small piece of finger bone.

show.text: A tiny fragment of a finger bone, laid on a lab tray, with Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains of Siberia in the background.

say.text: In 2010 the DNA from that bone was published. It matched neither Neanderthals nor us. It came from a group no one knew, now called Denisovans.

show.text: Denisovans

ask.q: What told scientists the finger bone came from a new group?
wrong: The tools lying next to it
ask.why: The DNA sequences showed the bone came from a previously unknown group of extinct humans.

say.text: Denisova Cave also has two dates. People used it from as long as 280,000 years ago. But the world only took notice in 2010.

show.text: Up to 280,000 years ago: people begin using the cave; 2008: finger bone dug up; 2010: DNA published and the cave becomes famous. Neanderthals and Homo sapiens used it too.

say.text: Denisovans are closer kin to Neanderthals than to us. Their line split off around 300,000 to 400,000 years ago. Yet we have only a handful of their bones.

show.text: Closer to Neanderthals than to us; split about 300,000 to 400,000 years ago; known from a handful of finger bones, molars and jaw pieces found in caves in Russia, China and Laos

say.text: One jaw came from Baishiya Karst Cave, high on the Tibetan Plateau. The jaw is about 160,000 years old. It was discovered in 1980.

show.text: About 160,000 years ago: the owner of the Xiahe jaw lived; 1980: jaw found at Baishiya Karst Cave; later: Denisovan DNA recovered from the cave sediments, the first outside Denisova Cave

say.text: Cousins also mixed with each other. 'Interbred' means had children together. A bone nicknamed Denny, from Denisova Cave, was a first-generation hybrid, about 90,000 years old.

show.text: Denny: a Neanderthal-Denisovan hybrid

ask.right: She was the child of one Neanderthal parent and one Denisovan parent
wrong: She was the oldest Denisovan known
ask.why: DNA in the bone showed she was a first-generation hybrid of Neanderthal and Denisovan.

say.text: Now our own species, Homo sapiens. The oldest fossils we know come from Jebel Irhoud, in Morocco. They are about 300,000 years old.

show.text: About 300,000 years ago

say.text: Jebel Irhoud has two dates too. People lived there some 300,000 years ago. Miners found the first skull in 1961, and its true age was only worked out in 2017.

show.text: 300,000 to 350,000 years ago: people live at Jebel Irhoud; 1961: miners digging for barite find a skull; 2017: new fossils and new dates published

say.text: Why was it missed for so long? The skull was first taken for an African Neanderthal. The mining also carted away rock, so the layers were partly lost. Burnt flint tools gave the new date.

show.text: Thought to be a Neanderthal; much rock lost to mining; new dating from burnt flint tools

ask.q: Who first found the Jebel Irhoud skull?
ask.right: Miners digging for the mineral barite
ask.why: Miners searching for barite stumbled on the skull in 1961.

say.text: The skulls look like a mix. The face and jaw are modern, like ours. The braincase is long, and the teeth are large, like older humans.

show.text: Looks like ours: the face and jaw | Looks older: a long braincase and very large teeth

ask.q: Which part of the Jebel Irhoud fossils looked most like ours?
ask.why: The fossils combine a modern-looking face with a more primitive, elongated braincase.

say.text: Other early finds lie across Africa. Florisbad, in South Africa, is about 260,000 years old. Omo Kibish, in Ethiopia, is at least about 230,000.

show.text: Oldest known Homo sapiens fossils by site

ask.q: Which of these three sites has the oldest fossils?
wrong: They are all the same age
ask.why: Jebel Irhoud is about 300 thousand years old, Florisbad about 260 thousand, Omo Kibish at least about 230 thousand.

say.text: That spread across Africa raises a big question. Did our species begin in one place, or many? Experts do not fully agree.

show.text: Two models of origin

say.text: First, an older debate. Did we begin in Africa and spread, or evolve from local ancestors around the world? DNA studies generally favoured Africa.

show.text: Began in Africa, then spread | Evolved from local ancestors across the globe (the 'multiregional' idea)

say.text: Now a newer debate, inside Africa. In 2018, Eleanor Scerri and colleagues argued that no single population or region made us. Many connected groups swapped genes and ideas.

show.text: Two drawings side by side: a tree with one trunk and many branches, and a braided river whose streams weave into and out of each other.

say.text: So, side by side. One view says a single population in one region became us. The pan-African view says several linked African groups did. A middle road is also argued.

show.text: Single African origin: one population, one region | Pan-African: many linked populations across Africa. Middle road: an 'extended single African origin'.

ask.q: In the pan-African picture, how did our species arise?
ask.right: From several connected African populations that swapped genes and culture
wrong: From one village in East Africa
ask.why: Pan-African supporters say our species emerged from admixture among numerous African populations, not a single origin.

say.text: The Jebel Irhoud team leans this way. They did not say those people were parents of everyone. They saw a large, interbreeding population across a green Sahara.

show.text: A map of Africa with a green Sahara, linking North, East and South African early Homo sapiens sites.

say.text: Now to the DNA. Neanderthals were the first extinct humans to have their genome decoded. It came from three bones in Vindija Cave, Croatia, about 44,000 years old.

show.text: The Neanderthal genome

say.text: Comparing it with living people gave a surprise. Many people with European or Asian ancestry carry a little Neanderthal DNA. Estimates run from about 1 to 4 percent. Many newer ones say 1 to 2.

show.text: About 1 to 2 percent

say.text: How did it happen? Around 60,000 years ago, early Homo sapiens spread out of Africa. They met Neanderthals and rarely had children with them. Groups that stayed in Africa never met them.

show.text: About 60,000 years ago: Homo sapiens spread to Asia and Europe; met Neanderthals; rare interbreeding; groups staying in Africa did not meet them

ask.q: According to the Smithsonian, why would Africans who stayed in Africa have had no first-hand contact with Neanderthals?
ask.right: Neanderthals lived in Europe and Asia, and those groups never met them
wrong: They had no DNA at all
ask.why: The Smithsonian says Homo sapiens populations that stayed in Africa would never have met Neanderthals.

say.text: But there is a twist. Newer work finds some Neanderthal DNA in Africans too, likely carried back by people who migrated into Africa. Some of the signal may also be a false alarm.

show.text: Neanderthal DNA reached Africa indirectly, by migrations back into Africa; one study found about a third as much as in Europeans and Asians; some 'Neanderthal' stretches may be modern-human DNA inside the Neanderthal genome

say.text: Denisovan DNA shows up most in Asia and the Pacific. In some island populations it reaches up to about 6 percent.

show.text: Share of the genome from other humans (approximate percent)

ask.q: Which group's DNA reaches up to about 6 percent in some Asian and Oceanic island populations?
wrong: No other human DNA at all
ask.why: Some Asian and Oceanic island populations have as much as 6 percent Denisovan DNA.

say.text: Some of this borrowed DNA helped. Tibetans likely got a high-altitude gene from Denisovans. It spread among people living high up.

show.text: A Denisovan gene for high altitude

say.text: A palaeoanthropologist at London's Natural History Museum put it neatly.

show.text: Neanderthals are partly our ancestors, even if we didn't evolve from them. (Chris Stringer)

ask.q: True or false: Homo sapiens evolved from Neanderthals.
ask.right: False. We share a common ancestor with them, and some of our DNA is Neanderthal
wrong: True. We descend directly from Neanderthals
False. We have no connection at all
ask.why: The Smithsonian says Neanderthals and modern humans evolved from a common ancestor between 700,000 and 300,000 years ago, and later interbred.

say.text: Last question. Why did Neanderthals vanish? All traces were gone by about 40,000 years ago. Four main ideas are still argued.

show.text: Population decline; changing climate; competition with Homo sapiens; absorption through interbreeding

say.text: Idea one is competition. A 2008 study found Neanderthals and our species used similar niches. It argued that our spread, not climate, caused the Neanderthals' range to shrink.

show.text: Competition

say.text: Idea two is climate. Some scholars say a changing climate pushed Neanderthals to extinction. A European team said that did not fit Italy.

show.text: Climate change

say.text: Idea three is being few. Neanderthal genomes show small groups and inbreeding. One model says small numbers alone could have been enough.

show.text: Small, isolated groups

say.text: Idea four is absorption. If small waves of Homo sapiens kept arriving and mixing, Neanderthal DNA could fade into ours. Other factors may also have played a part.

show.text: Absorption

ask.q: Do scientists agree on why Neanderthals disappeared?
ask.right: No. Several explanations are still debated, and more than one may have played a part
ask.why: Researchers describe the disappearance as a subject of intense debate, with several competing hypotheses, and other factors may also have contributed.

say.text: Let's gather it up. Several kinds of human shared the world. DNA shows some of them mixed. Where our own species began, and why Neanderthals vanished, are still open questions.

show.text: Neanderthals: cold-adapted, Mousterian tools; Denisovans: known mainly from DNA; Homo sapiens: at least 300,000 years old, found in Africa; DNA: about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal outside Africa; Open questions: one origin or many, and why Neanderthals vanished

ask.q: Which statement about most people living outside Africa today fits what we learned?
ask.right: A small share of their DNA, around 1 to 2 percent, comes from Neanderthals
wrong: None of their DNA comes from any other humans
Half of their DNA comes from Neanderthals
All of their DNA comes from Denisovans
ask.why: Genomes show a small Neanderthal share, about 1 to 2 percent in many estimates, in most people outside Africa.

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: The Sahara was green and early Homo sapiens groups spread across Africa. The Neanderthal line had already split from ours, about 550,000 years ago.
Neanderthals had evolved in Europe by about this time and were enduring winter cold and ice ages. In Ethiopia, Omo Kibish is at least about 230,000 years old.
At least four human species were alive: Homo luzonensis, Homo floresiensis, Homo neanderthalensis and Homo sapiens.
The earliest Homo sapiens populations were spreading from Africa to Asia and Europe, where they met Neanderthals.
All traces of Neanderthals had disappeared by about this time.

other_side.claim: Our species arose from a single population in one region of Africa.
other_side.other_view: Eleanor Scerri, Chris Stringer and colleagues argue that fossils, tools and genes fit a pan-African picture better. In this picture, many linked African populations swapped genes and culture, so our features arose at different times in different places. Other researchers say the real choice is between that view and an 'extended single African origin' with key changes in the braincase. The Jebel Irhoud team itself does not say those people were the direct ancestors of everyone alive.

other_side.claim: Neanderthals vanished mainly because Homo sapiens out-competed them.
other_side.other_view: Some scholars point to climate change instead, though a European team said it did not fit Italy. Others say small, inbred groups could have gone extinct on their own. Others argue they were gradually absorbed by repeated mixing with Homo sapiens, though one paper notes that the model does not prove this alone explains it. Many researchers think several factors combined.

The Smithsonian notes that the Shanidar 3 skeleton may have been buried by his group, or may have been covered by a rock fall from the cave roof. Britannica says evidence suggests burial and symbolic behaviour in Neanderthals more generally.

other_side.claim: Only people with ancestry outside Africa carry Neanderthal DNA.
other_side.other_view: The Smithsonian says Neanderthal DNA reached African-descended people indirectly, through ancient migrations back into Africa. One study found Africans carry about a third as much as Europeans and Asians, but its authors note that some stretches called Neanderthal may really be modern-human DNA inside the Neanderthal genome. Estimates are still being worked out.
